ECON1401.description:
Understanding the big picture is the first step to making informed decisions.  This course will empower students with economic principles and ideas that enable them to understand and debate how best to address pressing socioeconomic and political challenges.

You will participate in active reflection and debate about the discipline’s approaches, objectives, and limitations, about the history of economic development, and about how economics can contribute to framing and solving current challenges. Topics include economic growth and development in the long run, the relationships between political regimes and economic growth, the economics of conflict, the origin and persistence of social and economic inequalities, the exploitation of natural resources and climate change. 

By the end of the course, you will be able to critically evaluate economic arguments, understand how to address real-world problems through different lenses, and apply these perspectives to contemporary policy debates and everyday decision-making.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100
ECON1401.title: Economic Perspectives

ECON2101.description:
Decision-making by consumers, producers, and governments lies at the heart of economic analysis. It determines how scarce resources are allocated, how markets function, and how welfare is distributed across society.

The first half of this microeconomics course is devoted to the study of decision-making and the modelling of associated market behaviour. We then study how individual economic decisions interact in markets with varying degrees of competition, paying substantial attention to the comparative welfare outcomes produced by different market forms.

Additional topics include externalities, game theory and its applications, and asymmetric information. There is an emphasis on the use of analytical and mathematical models, which underpin much of current research in microeconomics.

By the end of the course, students will be able to apply core microeconomic models to analyse decision-making and market outcomes, critically evaluate efficiency and welfare implications across market structures, and use formal tools to address issues such as externalities, strategic interaction, and information asymmetries.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)
ECON2101.title: Microeconomics 2

ECON2102.description:
The macroeconomy of a country is a complex network consisting of millions of interacting pieces such as consumers, firms, banks, and government institutions. This course introduces students to some of the key models economists employ to understand how these pieces interact to generate economic growth, the business cycle, and inflation.  

This course covers models of aggregate income determination in open economies; theories of aggregate economic behaviour with respect to consumption, investment expenditures, and financial transactions; balance of payments and exchange rate analysis; theories of inflation and unemployment; introductory dynamic analysis; and theories of growth and business cycles. The models will be applied to the data and used to analyse the observed growth patterns across the world.  

By the end of the course, you will develop the tools, skills and knowledge base necessary to operate as a practicing macroeconomist.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: (ECON1102 or COMM1150) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)
ECON2102.title: Macroeconomics 2

ECON2103.description:
​​How do governments shape the business environment and influence the decisions of the businesses and individuals that interact in a market economy? This course examines the role of government intervention in the economy, including why markets left alone can fail, when intervention can be justified, and how policy choices affect societal outcomes. You ​will examine practical policy issues such as income redistribution, government-private sector interactions, and the evaluation of government programs.

​By the end of this course, you will have a firm foundation in government and policy analysis and be able to apply rigorous economic reasoning to analyse strategic interaction, policy design, and institutional choices. You will be equipped to contribute with precision and confidence to real-world policy debates.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100
ECON2103.title: Business and Government

ECON2107.description: The course delivers general theoretical and practical knowledge of labour markets and policy issues related to labour markets. The topics include labour supply and labour demand, theories and practice of wage determination, wage structures and wage differentials, labour productivity, labour mobility, labour market discrimination, and the role of government and unions in labour markets. The course also addresses macro-institutional outcomes, including labour force participation and evolution and change in labour markets. While drawing on the international literature and trends in international labour markets, the course places special emphasis on Australian labour market attributes and examples. You will acquire theoretical and practical tools to understand and analyse various labour markets phenomena.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisites: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1203 or COMM1190 or MATH1041 or MATH2801 or MATH2841 or MATH2901)
ECON2107.title: Modern Labour Markets: Theory and Policy

ECON2111.description: One out of ten people on Earth live on less than $2.15 USD per day (extreme poverty). This course explores the causes and correlates of global poverty, and investigates the policies used to address it. The approach of the course is microeconomic, meaning that we focus on individual and household behaviours, as well as market failures which lead to sub-optimal choices by these individuals. We will learn about measurement of poverty and inequality, the role of health and education in poverty, problems in credit, savings, and insurance markets, the causes and effects of migration, environmental degradation, and child labour. By the end of this course, students will be able to design innovative ways to assess whether a proposed development intervention is likely to successfully improve the welfare of its target population. This course will not cover macroeconomic topics, such as institutions, geography, growth, trade, or liberalization in any depth. This is not because these are not important topics, but rather because there are other courses in the School which are entirely dedicated to them. For students interested in those topics the following courses are recommended: ECON3110 (Development Economics), ECON3109 (Economic Growth, Technology, and Structural Change), ECON3116 (International Trade), and ECON3104 (International Macroeconomics).
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100
ECON2111.title: Introduction to Economic Development

ECON2112.description:
Game theory is a structured way to think about strategic interactions and it is fundamental to the understanding of modern business strategy.  

In this course, you will be introduced to the basic tools of Game Theory and its applications to business choices. We will cover normal form and extensive form games, games of perfect and imperfect/incomplete information, and will introduce equilibrium concepts such as Nash Equilibrium, Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium and Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium. We will also look at repeated games and the theory of reputation.  
 
By the end of the course, you will not only be equipped with an understanding of the basic principles of strategic analysis but will also easily navigate the issues related to integrating ethical and sustainable considerations into the application of abstract theory to specific real-world business challenges.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)
ECON2112.title: Game Theory and Business Strategy

ECON2126.description:
How do you do economics experiments "right" and why is it that "the way one does an experiment is unbelievably important", as a famous behavioural economist once noted?

In this course, we will talk about the experimental method in economics—and how it differs from methods in other social sciences—and will do so by reading widely cited articles. We shall discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the experimental method relative to other empirical social science methods such as analysis of administrative data, and we will document how it can be used to explore the robustness of the "homo economicus" assumption of a rational, selfish decision-maker used in many economic models.

By the end of the course, we will find that economic theory does a good job in many applications but that there are also important behavioural deviations from the model of “homo economicus”.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100
ECON2126.title: Principles of Experimental and Behavioural Economics

ECON2206.description:
What can the data tell us and how can we tell apart correlation and causality?

This course introduces the use of econometrics to explore and estimate economic relationships. Emphasis will be placed on cross-sectional data, and on understanding the conditions required for inferring causal relationships. We will tackle linear regression models, and give particular attention time series and panel data models, highlighting their relevance for economic analysis. Next, we will also consider extensions that address common data analysis complications, including heteroskedasticity, proxy variables, and other limitations. Practical computer-based exercises are integrated throughout, enabling students to gain hands-on experience with econometric software.

By the end of the course, you will have the skills to critically interpret empirical relationships and a foundation for more advanced courses in econometrics.
enrolment_rules_raw:
Prerequisite: ECON1203 or COMM1110 or ECON2403 or MATH1041 or MATH1231 or MATH1241 or MATH1251.
It is highly recommended that students who complete COMM1110 also complete COMM1190 before enrolling in this course.
ECON2206.title: Introductory Econometrics

ECON2209.description:
In an uncertain and data-rich business environment, making accurate predictions is both essential and challenging.

This course addresses how to transform data into reliable forecasts that support effective decision-making and strategic planning. It covers the practical use of econometric and statistical techniques applied in the business world. Building and evaluating forecasting models using time series data will be the focus of this course.

By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate and use reliable forecasting models based on sound economic principles.
enrolment_rules_raw:
Prerequisite: ECON1203 or COMM1110 or MATH1041 or MATH1231 or MATH1241 or MATH1251.
It is highly recommended that students who complete COMM1110 also complete COMM1190 before enrolling in this course.
ECON2209.title: Business Forecasting

ECON2403.description:
How can we critically assess the quality and evaluate the findings of research studies in social science?

This course will provide an introduction to the most common empirical methods used in scholarship across the social sciences.

Each topic will use a research article to illustrate different empirical methods, and also the range of topics that these methods are useful for analysing. Substantive topics will include: poverty, economic growth, public health, democracy, wage determination, and education.

By the end of the course, students will be well equipped to become sophisticated consumers of empirical social science research, rather than necessarily becoming producers of that work.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisites: PPEC1001 AND ECON1202 AND in program 3478 or 4797
ECON2403.title: Empirical Methods

ECON3101.description: This course delves into the theoretical underpinnings of financial crises, offering an advanced exploration of the factors that contribute to financial instability. Building on prior courses in microeconomics, macroeconomics, and game theory, this course will examine the role of market frictions, with a particular focus on asymmetric information, liquidity constraints, and incomplete markets. You will gain a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms leading to financial crises and the tools necessary to analyze and mitigate these events.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3101.title: Markets and Frictions

ECON3104.description:
In today’s global economy, national policies and outcomes are deeply interconnected.

This course introduces the core concepts and analytical tools of open-economy macroeconomics, providing a structured framework for examining how countries interact through trade, capital flows, and policy choices. It covers exchange rate determination, balance of payments, current account imbalances, international asset markets, and the role of fiscal and monetary policy in open economies. It also considers the functioning of different exchange rate regimes, the challenges of monetary unions, and the causes and consequences of international financial crises. Emphasis is placed on applying theory to contemporary issues and policy debates, enabling students to better interpret real-world events and understand the constraints and trade-offs faced by policymakers.

By the end of the course, students will appreciate how global forces shape national economic outcomes and long-term growth prospects.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2102
ECON3104.title: International Macroeconomics

ECON3106.description:
When so many economic decisions are taken by political actors, understanding the economy also means understanding the interactions between politics and economics.

This course covers theory, evidence and current issues at the intersection between economics and political science.

Topics considered include economic theories of the state, regime changes and revolutions, voting theory, interest group politics, corruption, the democratic peace, and electoral competition.

By the end of the course, you will have the skills relevant in understanding the delicate interplay between economics and politics.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3106.title: Politics and Economics

ECON3107.description:
​​Insurance is the oldest and most widespread form of financial risk management. Life insurers and annuity providers play a central role in modern financial markets by pooling longevity, mortality, and investment risks. The economic analysis of insurance markets draws on, and enriches, core theories of asset pricing, corporate finance, industrial organisation, and public economics.

This course uses the insurance sector—in particular life insurance and annuities—as a lens through which to understand financial economics. We begin with the institutional architecture of the insurance industry: products, balance sheets, data sources, and regulation. We then study how insurers price contracts. Next, we develop supply-and-demand models to analyse market outcomes in the variable annuity and life insurance markets and investigate how reinsurance and off-balance-sheet vehicles reshape risk. We conclude by examining insurers’ portfolio-choice decisions and their implications for asset prices and systemic risk.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3107.title: Economics of Finance

ECON3110.description:
​​Why do some countries grow and prosper while others remain trapped in poverty? Poverty and underdevelopment remain central global economic challenges. This course provides an in-depth exploration of competing explanations of underdevelopment and current strategies for promoting development. You will examine the roles of institutions, institutional change, markets, and policy in shaping development outcomes, with close attention to both domestic and international contexts. A key focus is the interaction between theory and evidence, including how to assess whether specific interventions are likely to improve welfare.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse major drivers of underdevelopment, assess development policies with theory and evidence, and identify credible pathways for improving outcomes.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101 and (ECON1102 or COMM1150)
ECON3110.title: Development Economics

ECON3116.description:
​​What determines who gains and who loses in global trade and how governments should respond? International trade shapes economic growth, wages, inequality, and the success or failure of businesses. This course provides a rigorous analysis of trade theory and trade policy, supported by empirical evidence. You will study comparative advantage, technology differences, factor endowments, and economies of scale, and how these forces influence trade patterns and income distribution. And you will evaluate the effects of key policy tools and develop practical problem-solving skills for trade analysis.

By the end of this course, you will be able to use trade models and empirical evidence to evaluate policy choices and their implications for key societal outcomes.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3116.title: International Trade Theory and Policy

ECON3121.description:
What drives the behaviour of firms and industry dynamics in the modern economic landscape?

This course studies the behaviour of firms and industry sectors, with a focus on competition outcomes and market dynamics. Through an exploration of market structures (including perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly), dynamic strategic interaction, price discrimination, product differentiation, advertising, entry and predation, it connects theoretical concepts with real-world relevance.

By the end of the course, you will develop a deep understanding of the economic forces at play in real-world markets and how they come together to drive economic policy.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3121.title: Industrial Organisation

ECON3123.description: This course studies the internal organisation of firms and other organisations. It provides a rigorous introduction to foundational theories, and then discusses applications to real-world managerial problems. How should incentives be designed in organisations? How should conflict within an organisation be resolved? When should organisations outsource and when should they produce internally? Why do organisations arise in market economies? Tools from game theory, information economics and contract theory are introduced and applied to analyse these (and other) questions.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or ECON2112
ECON3123.title: Organisational Economics

ECON3124.description:
​​Standard economic theory assumes that people have correct beliefs based on correct statistical reasoning, that they are narrowly self-interested, and that they manage to maximise their utility. Decades of experimental evidence suggest a more complicated picture. People systematically misperceive probabilities, cooperate with strangers in ways that sacrifice their own material payoffs, and make choices that they themselves deem suboptimal. Explaining these empirical regularities requires new theory.

In this course, students will study the core findings of behavioural economics, learn the formal theoretical frameworks developed to explain it, and build the empirical reasoning skills needed to critically evaluate competing accounts. Topics include reference-dependent preferences and prospect theory, intertemporal choice, risk preferences, bounded rationality, social preferences, behavioural game theory, and behavioural public policy.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to formulate behavioural hypotheses precisely, evaluate them using appropriate theoretical tools, and critically assess the evidence used to support or challenge them.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or ECON2112
ECON3124.title: Behavioural Economics

ECON3125.description:
In this course, we will explore the importance of health and human capital to individual well-being and economic growth. We will evaluate how natural, social, economic, and political environments affect the accumulation and stock of health and human capital and the ways in which health and human capital interact with one another. We will document the considerable inequality in health and human capital across society and consider ways in which policy may help reduce this inequality.
 
This course is largely devoted to exploring these relationships empirically. While it is interesting and instructive to document correlations between objects, like in-utero pollution exposure and birth weight or class size and academic achievement, our ability to influence outcomes, like birth weight and academic achievement, depends crucially on our ability to identify causal relationships between objects. To this end, this course will be structured around learning key methods of causal inference in empirical research.
enrolment_rules_raw: Pre-requisite: ECON2101 and ECON2206
ECON3125.title: Economics of Health and Human Capital

ECON3127.description:
The environment is one of the most important and most debated modern policy issues. This course provides an economic perspective on this debate. We will discuss the reasons behind why environmental problems exist, why unregulated markets sometimes fail in this context, and potential economic solutions to these problems, which include regulations, taxes, subsidies, and pollution permit trading schemes. We will also cover methods for determining the benefits and costs of environmental preservation. The course will equip you with the necessary knowledge to take part in the discussion about environmental policy from an economic perspective. 

Please note: this course was previously badged as ECON2127.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101
ECON3127.title: Environmental Economics

ECON3202.description:
Mathematics provides the formal language of modern economics, enabling us to rigorously analyse models, clarify assumptions, and derive precise insights into how economic systems function and respond to change.

This course provides a working knowledge of basic analysis, topology, and static and dynamic optimisation techniques applied in economics. Topics include logic and set theory, topological principles in Euclidean spaces, properties of real-valued functions (continuity, concavity, quasi-concavity), differentiation in multi-dimensional Euclidean spaces, classical optimisation with and without constraints, comparative statics, and envelope theorems.

By the end of the course, you will become familiar with a wide range of mathematical techniques as illustrated within mainstream theoretical applications such as consumer theory and game theory.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or MATH1231 or MATH1241
ECON3202.title: Mathematical Economics

ECON3203.description: The course offers a broad interdisciplinary perspective on econometrics, data science, statistical and machine learning methods through the lens of econometric theory and applications. The course emphasises the links between the theory, computational methods, and the application of the models to real examples. Being equipped with this knowledge will enable you to conduct a broad range of econometric modelling tasks.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON3209 or MATH2801 or MATH2901 or Enrolment in FINSBH Finance Co-Op Honours or Enrolment in FINSD1 Finance Co-Op
ECON3203.title: Econometric Theory and Machine Learning

ECON3206.description: This course provides the framework for modelling financial time series data, such as commodity/asset prices, interest rates or exchange rates. You will learn the key characteristics of financial data, concepts of volatility and risk, modelling time varying volatility, risk management, and relationships among financial series. The knowledge and methods acquired in this course are particularly useful and sought after in the public and private macroeconomic and financial sectors.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2209
ECON3206.title: Financial Econometrics

ECON3208.description:
Applied econometrics provides the tools to transform raw data into meaningful economic insight. It bridges theory and evidence, allowing us to rigorously test hypotheses, identify causal relationships, and inform real-world policy and business decisions.

This course extends econometric modelling using linear regression to cover nonlinear models such as logit and probit, regression methods for forecasting, and an introduction to the treatment of endogeneity (e.g. instrumental variable estimation). Special emphasis will be placed on the process and potential pitfalls of conducting and evaluating applied econometric research.

By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the necessary knowledge to be able to conduct your own econometric research using standard real-world economic and business data.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2206 OR (In Data Sciences and Decisions AND (MATH2831 or MATH2931))
ECON3208.title: Applied Econometric Methods

ECON3209.description:
Understanding the statistical backbone of modern econometric analysis is fundamental. It underpins how economists draw reliable conclusions from data, and critically evaluate the tools used in empirical research.

This course provides the foundations for modern econometric methods including probability theory, mathematical statistics, asymptotic theory, frequentist and Bayesian inference, underlying mathematical methods and an introduction to statistical computing. Mastering this course will give students a deeper understanding of the formal mathematical and statistical underpinnings of methods and knowledge commonly used in econometrics. Throughout the course, material will be presented in the context of simple models to concentrate on the concepts.

By the end of the course, you will have a rigorous grasp of the statistical principles that support econometric methods, providing the foundation needed for advanced data-driven economic analysis.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: ECON2206
ECON3209.title: Statistics for Econometrics

ECON3210.description:
​​How do economists turn complex data into credible evidence for decisions? The explosion of the amount, scope and availability of data has transformed how organisations make decisions. This course examines econometric and machine learning methods suited to data-rich environments, including regression, model selection and regularisation, regression trees, cross-validation, and natural experiments. You will compare how these methods perform across description, prediction, and counterfactual analysis tasks and how the key distinction between experimental and observational data must inform your analysis. You may also be introduced to newer data types such as textual, spatial, and network data.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods suited to a data-rich environment, critically assess identification and model choices, and communicate evidence with precision.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Pre-requisite: ECON2206 or ECON2209
ECON3210.title: Big Data Econometrics

ECON4100.description:
Understanding how individuals and firms make optimal decisions and how their interactions shape market outcomes is paramount. It underpins much of modern economics, helping explain and predict behaviour under different market structures and information conditions.

This course deals with individual optimal decision making and equilibrium. Fundamental topics covered include rational choice, utility maximisation, expenditure minimisation, production theory, and decision making under uncertainty. Partial equilibrium, game theory and non-competitive environments will also be covered. The course also explores economic environments with asymmetric information, including auctions and screening.

By the end of the course, you will be able to formally analyse strategic and non-strategic interactions in economic settings using microeconomic theory.
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4100.title: Advanced Microeconomic Analysis

ECON4103.description:
​​This is an advanced course in macroeconomic theory. The first part of the course will briefly review business cycle facts, real business cycle models, and useful tools and technique. The second part of the course will cover the New Keynesian approach to macroeconomics, covering topics such as monetary policy and inflation, the real effects of monetary policy, the advantages of credible policy commitments and monetary-fiscal interactions.

By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse macroeconomic dynamics with formal models and evaluate fiscal and monetary policy in a wide range of environments.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4103.title: Advanced Macroeconomic Analysis

ECON4106.description:
How can we measure the impact of economic interventions? Why do some policies succeed while others fail?

This course provides the powerful tools of causal inference that can answer such questions. It covers foundational methods for identifying causal effects—including randomised controlled trials, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity designs—to equip students with the skills to critically evaluate empirical research and conduct their own rigorous analyses.

By the end of the course, you will be able to evaluate and apply causal inference methods to real data to measure the effects of a wide range of policies and programs. Whether you are interested in public policy, labour markets, health, development, or finance, mastering causal inference will enhance their ability to make informed data-driven decisions and produce credible economic analysis.
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4106.title: Empirical Methods for Causal Inference

The student will undertake an independent and original research project leading to a thesis. The student will be supervised by at least one academic staff member from the School of Economics. Weekly honours seminars will be scheduled as part of this course to provide a forum in which students may present and discuss their research and obtain feedback from the other students and the seminar coordinator. ECON4201.description:
​​This course will provide you with an introduction to econometrics as it is applied in macroeconomics. Emphasis is on hands-on implementation of the methods covered in the course. Topics include macroeconomic data, linear and nonlinear time series models, practical issues with likelihood-based inference for these models, forecast evaluation, structural identification and use of micro data in empirical macroeconomics.

By the end of this course, you will be able to implement core macroeconometric methods, evaluate model assumptions, and draw defensible conclusions from aggregate data in order to undertake modern macroeconomic research.​
enrolment_rules_raw:
Pre-requisite: ECON4103
Assumed knowledge: Familiarity with matrix algebra, introductory statistics and econometrics. Prior Knowledge in Statistical software or programming languages will be useful.
ECON4201.title: Macroeconometrics

ECON4205.description:
This course covers advanced econometric methods for empirical research in applied microeconomics and related fields. You will study recent developments in widely used causal research designs, along with complementary approaches for policy and program evaluation. Applications are drawn from labour, development, political economy, education, and health. The course prepares you both to conduct research using state-of-the-art microeconometric methods and to critically evaluate empirical studies.

By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods, assess identification and model choices critically, and communicate evidence with precision.​
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4205.title: Microeconometrics

ECON4301.description: The main goal of this course is to provide you with a set of tools and knowledge that would enable you to critically read recent research papers and conduct your own original research in industrial organisation. In particular, we investigate how firms exercise market power in a variety of settings and how the government may curb the negative side effects of this through regulation. We will develop rigorous theoretical models maintaining their close connections to reality, elaborate on the economic logic and intuition behind the analyses, and discuss real-world implications. The course emphasises the importance of a theoretical understanding of strategic behaviour as the foundation for any practical application to industry.
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4301.title: Industrial Organisation

ECON4309.description: This course covers the theory and practice of economic measurement, including the measurement of key economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index, Gross Domestic Product and productivity growth. Approaches employed by international statistical agencies will be highlighted, along with the possibility that policy implications are often reliant on the choice of measurement techniques. The course will be technically rigorous, particularly in the use of microeconomic theory and econometric analysis and will draw on the latest international research developments.
enrolment_rules_raw: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)
ECON4309.title: Economic Measurement

EDST1003.description:
Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST2003

This course will engage in substantive exploration of key concepts, issues, and debates in language, literacy, and numeracy education, with particular reference to the language, literacy, and numeracy demands of the school curriculum and pedagogy. It draws on current research to identify likely areas of difficulty in language, literacy, and numeracy learning and discusses effective teaching strategies for learners, including English as an additional language/dialect learners.
EDST1003.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1003.title: Learning and Teaching: Language, Literacy and Numeracy

EDST1101.description: An introduction to the study of Educational Psychology which examines some aspects of development and of learning and instruction. Topics include: cognitive development, development of memory, the role of knowledge, problem solving and thinking, an introduction to instructional methods.
EDST1101.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1101.title: Educational Psychology

EDST1104.description: Do schools reduce or reinforce inequalities based on social, cultural, economic, and gender differences? What makes schools effective? Is education a public good or a private commodity? And what is the role of teachers, given that most research shows that schools only play a small role in explaining differences in how children do in school? By the end of this course, you should be able to discuss these four key questions. To do so, the course uses equity and social justice as key themes, and current research in educational sociology as evidence. You should complete the course with a critical understanding of how education, teachers and teaching interact with society.
EDST1104.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1104.title: Social Perspectives in Education

EDST1120.description: As a pre-service teacher this course provides you with knowledge about language and children’s language and literacy development. It will introduce you to the socio-functional theory of language; how children learn to mean nonverbally and verbally in early childhood; and how they perceive and create meanings orally, in written language and multimodally in primary school years. You will also explore differences and diversity in language and literacy development among bilingual children and children with language development delay. This course develops your synthesis and analytical skills to gather and evaluate research information about diverse children’s language and literacy development and analyse their needs.
EDST1120.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1120.title: Foundations of Literacy in Education

EDST1143.description: This course is designed to develop content knowledge that underpins the teaching of Human Society and its Environment. As a pre-service teacher you will engage with the necessary knowledge of Australian history and geography from a personal, local, national and global perspective; as well as engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander history and culture. You will develop content knowledge on the complex factors that have shaped Australia as a nation including British colonisation and Indigenous peoples, the development of democracy, and migration. You will investigate Australia’s identity through geographical concepts including place, environment, sustainability and change. You will also develop an understanding of geography as an interaction of people, places and environments across a range of scales. In this course you will develop knowledge of the skills required to acquire, process and communicate geographical information so as to better understand your role as responsibly informed global citizens. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing the skill of inquiry learning; being able to evaluate sources of data (both primary and secondary) as being reliable; identify bias and different perspectives; critically analyse findings; and draw and present conclusions using the appropriate contextual language in a range of communication forms.
EDST1143.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1143.title: Foundations of History and Geography in Education

EDST1200.description: As a preservice teacher, this introductory course provides you with a foundation to primary school scientific subjects and content. You will study concepts from the earth, space, biological, and physical sciences as they relate to the NSW Science K-6 Syllabus. This course also aims at developing your skills in communicating scientific findings and using technology for teaching.
EDST1200.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1200.title: Foundations of Science in Education

EDST1244.description: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with fundamental knowledge of The Arts in education. You will examine the basis on which learning in the visual and performing arts is grounded and the nature of students’ learning progression in the primary years of schooling. As a means for exploring and researching the disciplines of Visual Arts (including Media Arts), Music, Dance and Drama this course introduces you to a conceptual framework comprising the core and essential concepts of arts practitioner, artwork, audience and subject matter. You will learn to apply this framework in your own research of instances of arts practice and draw links to ways arts practices can be explained and interpreted. Through this research you will examine the different artforms in each discipline, how artists make artworks, how works are consumed and valued by different audiences on personal, community, symbolic and critical levels, and what artworks represent about our local, national and global societies, including Australian, Indigenous Aboriginal, Asian and international artists from historical and contemporary contexts. This course also develops your skills in critical interpretation when examining and interpreting different forms of art.
EDST1244.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1244.title: Foundations of the Arts in Education

EDST1311.description: This course provides preservice teachers with fundamental knowledge about engagement with, and discussions about, mathematical concepts which have been shown to be relatively challenging for students to understand. Concepts, aligning with the NSW syllabus include: proportional reasoning that underpins understanding of fractions, decimals, percentage, scale, similarity, and probability; variation and uncertainty; and generalisation. These concepts are relevant across the number and algebra, measurement and space, and statistics and probability curriculum strands. Preservice teachers will deepen their procedural knowledge and conceptual understanding of these mathematical concepts with an emphasis on building their confidence, and appreciation of the interconnected nature of mathematical content and the role of mathematics as a critical tool to address problems of global significance as well as personal relevance.
EDST1311.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST1311.title: Foundations of Mathematics

EDST2002.description:
Subject Area: Education

This course provides an opportunity for students to understand the structure and practice of education in NSW and appreciate the cognitive and societal factors that shape students' experiences and educational outcomes. Through a university-based seminar and 15 days of school-based fieldwork, the course enables students to observe and interact with a diverse range of students and professional educators and to actively reflect on the teaching and learning that is taking place in an educational institution.

Note: In order to undertake professional experience placements, you must: meet eligibility criteria; understand the policies and procedures that apply to professional experience placement; and provide satisfactory evidence of the NSW Mandatory Compliance Documentation (via InPlace).
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 72 UOC overall, including EDST1108 or EDST2009. Students must have passed LANTITE.
EDST2002.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2002.title: Professional Engagement

EDST2009.description:
Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST1108.

Teachers hold significant responsibilities to support, implement, respect, and learn from Indigenous perspectives in the classroom and in educational communities. In this course, you will learn how to enact this responsibility in classroom teaching, schooling, educational policy, and other professional practices. First, you will reflect on and locate yourself, your beliefs, and your perspectives as a future teacher in relation to land, language, culture, time, place, and relationships. You will then learn how this positionality impacts and informs your responsibility as a teacher, and helps you understand your students and their learning needs. Finally, you will engage with a range of Indigenous perspectives, research, theory, policy, and evidence to critically evaluate teaching resources and scenarios. This course will shape your professional practice in teaching in Australia or in other places that have their own histories of occupation, colonisation, or custodianship.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisites: 24 UOC overall, including EDST1101 and EDST1104, and either EDST1003 or EDST2003.
EDST2009.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2009.title: Indigenous Perspectives in Education

EDST2032.description: This course critically examines issues and innovations of contemporary relevance in state, national and global curricula. You will learn about the history and significance of curriculum innovations including learning progressions, general capabilities, and the integration of curriculum perspectives across disciplines and how these developments shape the role of the teacher, students, subject content and the broader purposes of schooling. Using social, philosophical and ethical frameworks you will evaluate the impact of these developments on education, discipline content, learning and teaching in the 21st century context.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1
EDST2032.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2032.title: Critical Issues in Education

EDST2044.description: Drawing on a range of contemporary motivational theories, this course considers their implications in the school context, with a focus on learning and teaching. These seminal theories serve as a foundation to an extensive empirical research base that enables students to learn about the nature of motivation in their own lives, with an emphasis on learning and educational settings. It also supports teachers to apply a range of practical strategies and techniques in their own pedagogy.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1
EDST2044.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2044.title: Motivation in Learning and Teaching

EDST2070.description: This course examines various theorizations of identity and culture, investigating how different conceptualizations of identity and culture constrain and/or enable particular educational responses to a range of sociopolitical and socioeconomic issues, at the societal, institutional, classroom and individual level.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1
EDST2070.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2070.title: Culture, Identity and Education

EDST2112.description: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with wide knowledge of mathematics content and mathematical applications. Special emphasis is put on your confidence, enthusiasm and finding meaning to learn, apply and teach mathematics. The course introduces you to the key mathematical concepts in the Australian curriculum, focusing on a few key understandings including reinforcing concepts considered earlier in the program (proportional reasoning, uncertainty and variation, and generalisation). You will also learn how the foundational mathematics skills can be scaffolded to move learners forward from early stages of learning towards increasingly sophisticated ideas. During the course you will become familiar with literature and learn to reflectively develop as a teaching professional.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1311
EDST2112.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2112.title: Early Learning of Mathematics

EDST2386.description:
In this course you will be provided with knowledge and skills in the field of Creative Arts in education. Experiences in the areas of Visual Arts, Music, Dance and Drama will develop your pedagogical knowledge and understanding of the distinctive nature of each discipline. You will develop a critical appreciation of the unique contributions the arts make to society and how these contributions can be engaged with, and interpreted in, the primary school classroom. Pedagogical principles, theoretical components and practice within Music, Visual Arts, Drama and Dance are examined and applied in the design and implementation of classroom practices in school settings.

Students should have completed EDST1244 before undertaking this course.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1244 and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program
EDST2386.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST2386.title: Creative Arts (K-6)

EDST3179.description:
In this course you will be introduced to the continuum of mathematics learning K-6, with reference to the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. There will be a focus on evaluating and teaching number concepts, taking into account the range of developmental understanding and student ability prior to school entry. The emphasis will be on the pedagogical approaches and teaching strategies suitable for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 which will develop your understanding of the three strands in the NSW Syllabus - Number & Algebra, Measurement & Geometry, and Statistics & Probability. There will also be a focus on the formative and summative assessment strategies needed to evaluate student progress in the early years. 

Students should be enrolled in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program and have completed EDST2112 before undertaking this course.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST2112, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST3179.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3179.title: Mathematics 1 (K-2)

EDST3182.description:
In this course, you will learn how to teach children how to read. Among the range of approaches to early reading instruction, evidence best supports reading instruction that is explicit, systematic, and sequenced. Such instruction includes the components of phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, and oral language development. You will learn what these skills are, how to teach them, how to assess them, and how to respond with evidence-based interventions to develop early reading skills.

Students should have completed EDST1120 before undertaking this course. Students should not be enrolled in EDST3221 and EDST3200 before completing EDST3182.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1120, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST3182.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3182.title: Early Reading Instruction

EDST3221.description: As a pre-service teacher, this course prepares you with curriculum, content and pedagogical knowledge for teaching composition of oral, written and multimodal texts in the K-6 English syllabus. You will learn about children’s writing development processes from oral language, to letter, word and text composition. You will also learn about contemporary text creating practices required in the 21st century curriculum including drafting, composing and publishing. The course also introduces you to pedagogies to assist primary school students develop their creating competence including computer assisted pedagogies. In this course, you will learn to compose model texts to be used as teaching resources, analyse and evaluate teaching resources, and develop a program for teaching and assessing writing/creating with detailed lesson plans and activities to cater for learner diversity.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1120, and either EDST3182 or EDST6782, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program
EDST3221.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3221.title: Curriculum, Pedagogy and Assessment - Teaching Writing (K-6)

EDST3283.description: This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment strategies, classroom management and development/selection of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of human society and its environment in the primary school classroom. Students will engage in the selection/development/evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of key concepts in human society and its environment.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1143, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST3283.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3283.title: Human Society and its Environment (K-6)

EDST3284.description:
This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment and classroom management strategies relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary school classroom. You will engage in the selection, development, and evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary (K-6) classroom. The course aims to enable you to harness children’s natural curiosities to develop interest, enthusiasm, and knowledge for science and technology. 

Students should have completed EDST1200 before undertaking this course.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST1200, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program
EDST3284.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3284.title: Science and Technology (K-6)

EDST3380.description:
In this course you will build on the knowledge, skills and understanding developed in EDST3179 Mathematics 1. The focus is on Stages 2 and 3 in the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. You will engage in findings from contemporary research to explore pedagogical strategies suitable for developing student understanding of numeracy; and how this understanding supports mathematical understanding across Stages 2 and 3. Formative and summative assessment strategies suitable for this age group are included, along with skills needed to identify and analyse a range of data about students’ progress. You will also consider how to support learners as they transition to Stage 4 in Mathematics.

Students should have completed EDST1311, EDST2112, and EDST3179 before undertaking this course. The course is complemented by a minimum of 5 days supervised professional experience.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: EDST3179 or EDST6779, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST3380.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST3380.title: Mathematics 2 (3-6)

EDST4002.description: As a preservice teacher, this course provides you with essential knowledge of Physical Education skill learning and primary school Health content for teaching PDHPE in the Australian classroom. Through a practical approach, the course introduces you to the 12 Fundamental Movement Skills (FMS). You will learn the theoretical underpinnings of key elements of Health and Personal Development, with a focus on sensitive topics. This course also develops your understanding of how each of the focus areas of PDHPE (Movement Skill and Physical Activity; Respectful Relationships and Safety; Identity, Health and Wellbeing; and Self-Management and Interpersonal Skills) are interrelated and how they combine to create a holistic approach to teaching PDHPE.
EDST4002.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4002.title: Foundations of Primary School Personal Development, Health and Physical Education

EDST4080.description: This course provides an overview of the field of special and inclusive education. It surveys the characteristics, training, and educational needs of students with a disability. The course emphasizes accommodating students with a disability in inclusive settings, including legal mandates and regulations; characteristics and educational needs of students with a disability; and evidence-based practices which can be used with these students in the general education classroom. By the end of the course, students will have a broad overview of the field and its key concepts, issues, and the relevant Department of Education policies. They will be conversant with the main categories of students with a disability and know some ways of accommodating for these students in the inclusive classroom.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 78 units of credit overall, including EDST2002, and enrolment in an Education Secondary program OR Enrolment in Bachelor of Education Primary (Honours) or Bachelor of Education Primary.
EDST4080.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4080.title: Special Education: Inclusive Strategies

EDST4084.description: Classroom management and student engagement is the number one concern of all new teachers. This course provides students with both the theoretical and practical applications of classroom management principles necessary for new teachers to make professional decisions with respect to classroom management concerns. The focus of this course is on creating an engaging classroom environment and on positive behaviour interventions and support, including the evidence-based practices crucial to effective classroom management.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 78 UOC overall, including EDST2002, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program. Or 42 UOC overall, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST4084.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4084.title: Managing the Classroom Environment

EDST4096.description: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the field of gifted education, delving into talent development and best practices for identifying and responding to the needs of gifted and talent students. Students will explore (a) models of giftedness, (b) domain-specific and general characteristics of gifted learners, (c) underachievement, (d) teacher responsibilities, and (e) differentiated instruction and curriculum design for all learners.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 78 UOC overall, including EDST6760, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program or 4072 Education (Primary) program.
EDST4096.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4096.title: Responding to Gifted and Talented Students

EDST4501.description: A 6 UOC thesis in Education to be completed as part of the 30 UOC of thesis component in the Honours Program. Students are also required to complete 18 UOC of coursework.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4501.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4501.title: Education Honours

EDST4502.description: A 12 UOC thesis in Education to be completed as part of the 30 UOC of thesis component in the Honours Program. Students are also required to complete 18 UOC of coursework.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4502.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4502.title: Education Honours

EDST4503.description: An 18 UOC thesis in Education to be completed as part of the 30 UOC of thesis component in the Honours Program. Students are also required to complete 18 UOC of coursework.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4503.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4503.title: Education Honours

EDST4505.description: This course provides students with an overview of the philosophical, practical, and ethical issues involved in designing and conducting research in education. Students will be introduced to the need to conceptualize research at multiple levels, including epistemology, theory, approach, and strategy. The course will also focus on data collection and analysis, and the interpretation of data.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4505.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4505.title: Honours Research Methodology

EDST4506.description: A seminar course for honours students in the School of Education preparing students for the writing of an honours thesis. Topics include using library resources for honours students including research consultation and access to databases; structuring and writing a thesis, gaining ethics approval for collecting data; constructing a conceptual framework for a thesis; researching and writing literature reviews; the role of theory in research and the use of theory in framing and conducting a research project in Education; planning and managing a research project; formal requirements for the thesis structure and presentation.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4506.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4506.title: Honours Seminar 1

EDST4507.description: A seminar course for honours students in the School of Education preparing students for the writing of an honours thesis. Topics include structuring and writing a thesis, research design; researching and writing thesis chapters; planning and managing a research project; thesis presentation.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program
EDST4507.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST4507.title: Honours Seminar 2

EDST5180.description: This course is the first research course in the B.Ed Primary program and will provide you with an understanding of research in education. This will be achieved through exploring different research traditions, research ethics, the research process including issues of validity and reliability, a variety of both qualitative and quantitative research approaches and methodologies used in educational research, the management and analysis of data, and critical thinking and different genres of writing education research and findings. The course will prepare you for conducting your own research project including issues of identifying and formulating a research question; and selecting and applying appropriate research approaches and methods of inquiry. Successful completion of this course is one of the conditions for you to pursue your enrolment into the B.Ed Primary with embedded Honours program.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 78 UOC overall, including enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program
EDST5180.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST5180.title: Educational Research

EDST6700.description:
This is a hybrid course. It is available to both undergraduate and postgraduate students. The course content, delivery and assessment will be identical for both groups of students.

In this course, you will begin to learn how to teach Chinese in secondary contexts. You will use relevant syllabus documents to develop innovative and engaging lesson plans. You will learn and practise a range of effective teaching strategies designed to engage a diversity of learners in a safe and supportive classroom environment. You will learn how to use digital and other innovative resources to assess and improve learning in the discipline and to develop language, literacy and numeracy skills across the curriculum. Through self and peer evaluation you will also learn how to present yourself in a professional, supportive manner.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 78 units of credit overall, including EDST2002, and enrolment in program 4053 or 4054
EDST6700.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST6700.title: Chinese Method 1

EDST6715.description:

In this course, you will begin to learn how to teach Business Studies in secondary contexts. You will use relevant syllabus documents to develop innovative and engaging lesson plans. EDST6758.description:
This is a hybrid course. It is available to both undergraduate and postgraduate students. The course content, delivery and assessment will be identical for both groups of students.

In extension to learning some basic skills and concepts in music education, students undertaking this course will think deeply about some of the most critical issues facing music educators. Content knowledge will be integrated in pedagogy and linked to professional issues unique to music educators. This course is designed with a view to students eventually becoming excellent teachers who are able to continue to improve the quality of music education in Australia.

EDST6758.title: Extension Music Method 2

EDST6760.description:
This is a hybrid course. It is available to both undergraduate and postgraduate students. The course content, delivery and assessment will be identical for both groups of students.

In this course you will develop a range of teaching skills and understandings essential to plan for and manage successful classrooms. You will complete an orientation and a range of online activities, followed by a 4-week (i.e., 20 consecutive days) supervised professional experience placement in a NSW school. Through ongoing observation, supervised teaching, and contribution to the wider school community, the course ensures you work towards the achievement of the national standards for a graduate teacher. You will gain an understanding of the range of activities that occur both inside and outside the classroom and the roles of the teaching and non-teaching staff within the school.

Note: In order to undertake professional experience placements, you must: meet eligibility criteria; understand the policies and procedures that apply to professional experience placements; and provide satisfactory evidence of the NSW Mandatory Compliance Documentation (via InPlace).
enrolment_rules_raw:
Prerequisite: Enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program and EDST2002, EDST4084, and 12 UOC Method 1 courses. Students must have passed LANTITE. See Additional Enrolment Constraints for the subject content knowledge requirements to be eligible for placement.
Or enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program and EDST2002, and either EDST3179 or EDST6779, and either EDST3182 or EDST6782. Students must have passed LANTITE.
EDST6760.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST6760.title: Professional Experience 1

EDST6765.description:
This is a hybrid course. It is available to both undergraduate and postgraduate students. The course content, delivery and assessment will be identical for both groups of students.

Subject Area: Education

In this course you will complete your final 9-week (45 days) professional experience block in a NSW school which you have not been involved with previously. During your placement you will be provided with increasing opportunities for autonomy, responsibility and accountability through a gradual shift from direct in-class supervision to program supervision by the Supervising Teacher(s) as you move into the internship phase of the course.
enrolment_rules_raw:
Prerequisite: 180 UOC overall, including EDST4080, EDST4096, EDST6760, 24 UOC Teaching Method courses, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program. See Additional Enrolment Constraints for the subject content knowledge requirements to be eligible for placement.

Or 180 UOC overall, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.
EDST6765.faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
EDST6765.title: Professional Experience 2/Internship
