This course is the higher version of MATH3811, with topics explored at greater depth.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATH2931 or MATH2831(DN).
MATH3911.title: Higher Statistical Inference

MATH3945.description:
This undergraduate course provides the theoretical foundation and methodological background for the analysis of categorical response data. Through a series of lectures and labs, a range of topics will be introduced including the Bernoulli trial, the analysis of contingency tables, and generalised linear models including logistic and Poisson regression. Statistical computing is an integral part of this course.

This course is jointly taught at two levels: MATH3945 is for 3rd year undergraduate students and MATH5945 for Honours & Masters students. Lectures will be conducted simultaneously for both streams, but tutorial classes and computer labs will be conducted separately for the two groups.
MATH3945.title: Categorical Data Analysis

MATH4001.description:
This course is only available to students enrolled in an Honours Program in the School of Mathematics and Statistics and enrolment must be approved by the School’s Honours Coordinator.

This course is taken three times over three consecutive terms (3 x 6 UoC for a total of 18 UoC). It forms the research thesis project component of the honours streams for programs within the School of Mathematics and Statistics. The three instances of the course form part of the one thesis project.
The student will undertake independent study in the appropriate area of applied mathematics, pure mathematics, physical oceanography, or statistics according to their honours stream. The student will be supervised by at least one member of the academic staff of the School of Mathematics and Statistics, possibly jointly with an academic external to the School, or, with the permission of the Head of School, a suitable other person in a non-university research position. The student will write a thesis, give an oral seminar presentation on the thesis to the appropriate department, and attend an oral assessment (viva voce) with examiners to elaborate on their thesis topic.

The final thesis will be assessed on four major areas: exposition, literature coverage, critical analysis and insight originality.
The weighting of these components will depend on the type of thesis which is determined by discussion between the student and supervisor(s) when the topic is chosen. All theses are expected to address all four areas.


Regular honours meetings will be timetabled as part of the thesis courses and participation will be assessed. The main purpose of these meetings is to provide a forum for honours students to give an oral presentation of their work to, and receive feedback from their peers and the honours coordinators. The meetings will also be used for other honours training purposes on more general mathematical and statistical skills, such as literature, research methodology, writing, presentation, or AI skills.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolled in MATH Honours stream
MATH4001.title: Mathematics and Statistics Honours Thesis

MATH6781.description:
This course introduces mathematical modelling and data analysis for biological and biomedical systems. The course is suitable for students with an interest in the real-world application of differential equation modelling. Examples of the biological systems studied in the course include: population dynamics, the spread of infectious diseases, drug delivery and metabolism, biochemical reactions, the formation of animal coat patterns, and the growth of tumours. The emphasis in this course is on the development of the governing model equations, and on the analysis and interpretation of the model solutions. Methods for computer simulation of the model equations will be demonstrated but students’ knowledge of these methods will not be assessed in the course.
In addition to lectures, the course will feature tutorials and workshops. Weekly tutorials require the class to solve a series of mathematical problems that build upon the lecture material. Workshops (several during the course) further consolidate the lecture material as the class makes use of modelling, analysis and computer simulations to perform in-depth studies of particular biological applications.
Assumed Knowledge:
Completion of two years of an undergraduate degree in mathematics or statistics.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: 12 units of credit in Level 2 Mathematics courses including: MATH2121 or MATH2221 or both MATH2019 and MATH2089 or both MATH2069 and MATH2099
MATH6781.title: Biomathematics

MATS1101.description:
This course introduces the fundamentals of Materials Science and Chemistry used in engineering. The different classes of materials used in engineering designs are introduced, and their basic structural, mechanical and functional properties are defined, and the mechanical properties are measured in laboratory activities. The relationships between a material’s underlying structure and its properties are explored. The ways in which materials fail within engineering settings are identified.

The chemistry part of the course builds on an elementary knowledge of chemistry (equivalent to one year of high school chemistry, such as Year 11 chemistry, or CHEM1001 at UNSW) to explore the structure of atoms leading to an understanding of the properties of materials at an atomic and molecular level. This knowledge is applied to understanding chemical bonding and intermolecular forces which determine the engineering properties of materials. General principles of chemical equilibrium are developed and applied to chemical reactions involving acids and bases and organic molecules to understand the reaction materials can undergo.

The course will consist of lectures, laboratories and tutorials split between the two disciplines: Materials Science and Engineering and Chemistry. This course is intended for engineering students to take early in their programs.

exclusions.title: Design in Application of Materials in Science and Engineering
Introduction to Materials for Engineering Applications
Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering

MATS1101.title: Engineering Materials and Chemistry

MATS1110.description: This course introduces Engineering students to the field of Materials Science and Engineering. Throughout society, different materials are chosen for various applications. How and why given materials are selected, is a key step in the Engineering process. In this course, students will learn about the different classifications of materials, how their atomic structure and processing leads to the desirable properties needed for industry. Laboratory work will be used to examine the testing techniques employed by materials engineers to determine the properties and which processes are best suited for a given material. Students will be challenged to select the correct material for a real-world problem through their understanding of mechanical, chemical and structural properties of materials. The delivery of course content is through a combination of lectures, tutorials, laboratories and project work. No prior science knowledge is required to undertake this course.

exclusions.title: Design in Application of Materials in Science and Engineering
Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering

MATS1110.title: Introduction to Materials for Engineering Applications

MATS1192.description:
This first-year (Level 1) introductory course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the structure and properties of materials, highlighting their major positive impact on society, particularly in structural, biomedical, and transport applications.

The course commences with the factors influencing the microstructure of materials, and the impact of microstructure on the properties and performance of engineering materials (metals, ceramics, polymers and composites). The course then covers topics on the micromechanisms of elastic and plastic deformation, and fracture mechanisms for ductile and brittle materials. It also introduces students to phase equilibria and how temperature and composition affect the expected phases in a material, which are further understood with the use of phase diagrams.

Students will gain an insight into why materials science and engineering matters via interviews with academic staff in the school about their current research, and visits to major industrial materials companies in New South Wales. Introductory materials laboratories will allow students to test and characterise materials and analyse data related to material properties.

This is the introductory materials core course for students in the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. Successful completion of the course is a requirement for some Level 2 materials courses in these programs.

The course content will be delivered through a series of standard and flipped lectures and tutorials.

A knowledge of high-school level chemistry and physics (NSW HSC Year 11 or equivalent) will provide a strong foundation for the course.

equivalents.title: Design in Application of Materials in Science and Engineering

exclusions.title: Introduction to Materials for Engineering Applications

MATS1192.title: Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering

MATS2001.description:
This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the physical properties of materials and their application in the design and operation of functional devices. These devices include critical components found in electric vehicles, computers, televisions, mobile telephones, and more.

The course begins with a discussion of the limitations of classical physics in describing physical properties. Elementary quantum and statistical mechanics are then introduced to provide a more accurate description, demonstrated firstly by explaining electronic conduction in materials and their categorisation as insulators, semiconductors, metals, and superconductors.  Students will also learn about intrinsic (pure) and extrinsic (doped) semiconductors and the concept of selective doping to create p-n junctions, the essential building blocks of electronic devices.

The course then focuses on magnetic materials, with particular emphasis on their ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic properties, including the origin of spontaneous magnetisation, magnetic domains, magnetic anisotropy, and magnetic hysteresis.  Thermal properties are also discussed, focusing on the roles of phonons and electrons on heat capacity, thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, and thermoelectricity. Lastly, students will learn about optical properties, and the interaction of materials with light through absorption, transmission, refraction, and reflection.

Examples of technologically significant electronic, magnetic, thermal and optical devices are provided to demonstrate the application of the fundamental principles presented in the course.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.

The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, in-person laboratory classes, assignments, and tests.

Previous knowledge of first year calculus, physics, and chemistry is required.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATH1131 or DPST1013 or MATH1141 and MATH1231 or DPST1014 or MATH1241 and PHYS1121 or PHYS1131 or DPST1023 and CHEM1011 or CHEM1031 or DPST1031 or CHEM1811
MATS2001.title: Physical Properties of Materials

MATS2003.description:
This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the principles and applications of the main analysis techniques for characterising the structure and composition of crystalline and amorphous materials.

The course covers topics on specimen preparation, crystallography, diffraction theory, and associated diffraction and scattering techniques, optical microscopy, electron microscopy, spectroscopy, image analysis, and methods for quantifying microstructural features.  Laboratory classes complement the lectures to equip students with basic practical skills in specimen preparation and operation of selected characterisation instruments and related software, as well as cultivating safe working practices in the laboratory. 

The course will provide the intellectual framework for other core and elective courses that require knowledge of the structure-property relationships in materials.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. It is also suitable for science and engineering students who need a fundamental understanding and practical skills in the characterisation of materials. 

The course includes weekly lectures, self-learning online activities, and in-person laboratory classes.

Previous knowledge of introductory materials science and engineering is recommended.
MATS2003.title: Materials Characterisation

MATS2004.description:
This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering extends on the fundamentals of mechanical behaviour of engineering materials introduced in MATS1192 Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering.

The course provides a systematic and quantitative treatment of how materials respond to stresses and strains. Key topics include stress, strain, axial and multiaxial loading, and the analysis of stresses in components under axial, torsional, bending, and transverse shear stresses. The course extends this knowledge to complex stress states in combined loading scenarios, employing numerical and graphical methods, such as Mohr’s circle leading to failure criteria (e.g. Tresca, von Mises).

The course then covers the mechanical properties and behaviour of engineering materials, examining metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites, and exploring their elastic and plastic deformation mechanisms at atomic, molecular, and microscopic levels. Material failure and its prediction are covered, including crack propagation, ductile and brittle modes of failure, yield criteria, creep and fatigue. The influence of factors such as strain rate and temperature on mechanical behaviour is analysed.

The course provides a solid foundation for more advanced level courses covering the structure-property-processing-performance relationships of specific classes of materials.  

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.

Teaching methods include lectures, tutorials, and laboratory classes to provide hands-on experience with mechanical testing.

Previous knowledge of first-year calculus is recommended.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS1101 or MATS1192 or DPST1061 or MATS1110
MATS2004.title: Mechanical Behaviour of Materials

MATS2005.description: This course introduces the fundamentals of fluid flow and heat transfer, and their applications in materials engineering. The fluid flow section starts with the concepts of fluids and static fluids, followed by the description of various fluid flows and their governing equations. Finally, the principle and applications of Bernoulli’s equation are discussed. The heat transfer section introduces the mechanisms, governing equations and applications of conductive heat transfer, convective heat transfer and thermal radiation. The course includes face-to-face lectures, in-class quizzes and weekly tutorials.
MATS2005.title: Introduction to Fluid Flow and Heat Transfer

MATS2006.description:
This course provides an introduction to reaction kinetics, including elementary and non-elementary reactions, reaction order, activation energy, Arrhenius law, irreversible and reversible reactions, degree of reaction; heterogeneous reactions, kinetics of solid state-gas (fluid) reactions, elementary steps, rate-controlling steps, intrinsic kinetics.
Through a series of lectures and a laboratory class, the course also explores: diffusion and mass transfer in the gas and fluid phases, solid state diffusion, atomistics of diffusion, Fick's first and second laws; thin film solution and tracer diffusion measurements, semi-infinite and infinite diffusion couples - diffusion in a concentration gradient; temperature effects; surface, grain boundary and dislocation pipe diffusion; diffusion in ionic solids, interdiffusion and the Kirkendall effect, measurement of variable diffusion coefficients and compares thermodynamics vs. kinetics in an applied environment.
MATS2006.title: Diffusion and Kinetics

MATS2008.description:
This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the fundamental principles of thermodynamics and their application in understanding the physical and chemical behaviour of pure substances, solutions, and multiphase systems relevant to the discipline.

The course begins with an overview of essential thermodynamic concepts and the three laws of thermodynamics. Building on this foundation, students learn about thermodynamic relations, gas-solid equilibria, ideal and non-ideal solutions, colligative properties, phase stability and the molecular basis of thermodynamics. Selected topics on materials thermodynamics illustrate these principles, including the oxidation and reduction of metals and oxides, thermodynamics of polymer solutions, solubility of gases in liquids and solids, lattice defects, and interfacial phenomena. The second part of the course focuses on phase equilibria, covering the types of unary and binary phase diagrams, Gibbs phase rule, lever rule, and experimental and computational tools for constructing phase diagrams. The practical application of binary phase diagrams will be utilised for designing microstructures in technologically significant material systems.

The course provides students with a solid foundation in basic thermodynamic principles and phase stability, preparing them for advanced courses requiring these essential concepts.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.

Lectures, tutorials and laboratory activities are the primary modes of delivery.

Previous knowledge of first-year chemistry, physics and calculus is recommended.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: CHEM1011 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1811 or MATS1101 or DPST1031
MATS2008.title: Thermodynamics and Phase Equilibria

MATS2009.description:
This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the processes by which heat, mass and momentum move through and between materials and systems of relevance to the materials engineering discipline. 

The course commences with an overview of fluid properties, including a detailed comparison between Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, followed by a description of fluid mechanics, mechanical energy balance of flow and Bernoulli’s equation. It then covers the mechanisms of heat transfer by thermal conduction, convection, and radiation, through to the mechanisms of diffusion of atoms, ions and molecules in materials, the application of Fick’s laws of diffusion, and specific examples of diffusion in solids, including the role of crystalline defects as enhanced diffusion pathways. Students will apply these fundamental principles of transport phenomena to areas of technological importance in materials science and engineering, including fluid flow during casting, polymer processing, the design of heat-resistant barriers and heat treatment processes, oxidation of metals, and doping of semiconductors.

The course provides a solid foundation for those higher-level courses requiring knowledge of transport processes.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.

The course includes lectures, weekly tutorials, assignments and in-class quizzes.

Previous knowledge of first-year calculus and chemistry is required.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATH1231 or MATH1241
MATS2009.title: Transport Processes in Materials Engineering

MATS3001.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts that govern the micromechanical behaviour of metals and alloys, and the principles involved in designing alloy microstructures with enhanced properties and performance.

The course commences with an overview of the various types of crystalline defects in metals, with a particular focus on the structure and properties of dislocations and their response to external stimuli such as stress and temperature. This is followed by a discussion of dislocation theories of strengthening through their mutual interactions (work hardening), and their interactions with key microstructural features such as solute atoms, precipitates, dispersoids, and grain boundaries. The course then covers the effects of deformation temperature and strain rate on dislocation dynamics, microstructural evolution, and mechanical behaviour.  The foregoing concepts are used to illustrate the principles involved in designing alloy microstructures for low- or high-temperature strength, creep resistance, and superplastic formability, as well as for optimising industrial metal working processes such as rolling, forging, and extrusion, with a focus on ethical and environmentally responsible production practices.  Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on applying these principles to explain the development and processing of key commercial ferrous and non-ferrous alloys used in structural and functional applications.

The course includes lectures, tutorials, assignments, and tests, as well as interactive online tutorials where students have the opportunity to practice applying their theoretical knowledge, solve problems, deepen their comprehension of the subject matter, and receive feedback on their learning.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.  It also provides foundational, metals-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design.

Previous knowledge of crystallography and mechanical behaviour of materials is required.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2004
MATS3001.title: Micromechanisms of Mechanical Behaviour of Metals

MATS3002.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the interplay between processing, (micro)structure, and properties of technical and functional ceramic materials, with a focus on their responsible manufacture and use across a wide range of technological and societal applications, including building and civil construction, energy storage and conversion, computing and electronics, nuclear, and health and biomedicine.  The successful use of ceramics in these applications is critically dependent on the composition-(micro)structure-property correlations of the materials which, in turn, are determined by the processes used to manufacture them.

The course begins with an overview of the fundamental behaviour of ceramics, focusing on how composition and microstructure influence their mechanical, physical and chemical properties.  The course then examines the main routes for fabricating ceramics through coverage of conventional key steps including raw materials, powder preparation, powder compaction and dry forming, wet forming, plastic forming, and sintering (conventional and advanced), conventional fabrication routes (slip casting, sintering, sol-gel etc).  Advanced routes (hot isostatic pressing, CVD, sputtering, additive manufacturing etc.) for ceramics in both bulk and thin film forms for different applications are also examined.  Students learn about the critical role of processing methods in determining ceramic microstructures, properties, and performance, and how these materials are designed and engineered for specific products and devices across diverse industries. The principles of ternary phase equilibria are introduced to support understanding of the relationships between composition, processing, and phase evolution in industrially-significant ceramic systems.  A focus throughout the course is analysis of processing problems and prescribing evidence-based solutions.

The course is completed as weekly lectures, self-learning online activities, assignments, and in-person laboratory classes targeted towards solving ceramic processing related problems and challenges.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.  It also provides foundational, ceramics-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design.

Previous knowledge of crystallography, thermodynamics, and binary phase equilibria is required.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2008
MATS3002.title: Fundamentals of Ceramic Processing

MATS3003.description: This is an elective course for 3rd or 4th year undergraduate students of Materials Science & Engineering focusing on the fundamentals of process and physical metallurgy principles, some of which have been introduced in 1st year (e.g., in MATS1192 ‘Design and Application of Materials in Science and Engineering’).  The first part of this course focuses on traditional and modern processes required to refine iron from ores into iron and steel. Students will also learn how to describe and evaluate recent major developments in the steel industry, and how to apply this knowledge to identify areas for improvement in terms of the sustainability of these processes. The second part focuses on the physical metallurgy of simple steels before exploring the process metallurgy of specialty alloys and non-ferrous alloys. Prior knowledge of the basic principles governing processing-microstructure-property relationships of alloys will be expanded to consider various factors affecting the final properties of semi-finished metal products such as thermo-mechanical treatments, segregation, complex heat treatments, additive processing routes, workflows during non-ferrous processing, energy consumption, and other environmental aspects. This is a face-to-face course with live lectures and tutorials.
MATS3003.title: Engineering in Process Metallurgy

MATS3004.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with a fundamental and practical understanding of polymer science and engineering, the importance of polymers in engineering and society, and the ethical and environmental considerations associated with their manufacture and use.

The course begins with a review of polymer classification, followed by a revision of basic organic chemistry and an introduction to polymer chemistry, focusing on raw materials and polymer synthesis. Key polymerisation techniques, including free radical, ionic, and condensation methods, are presented with attention to their underlying mechanisms and kinetics. Students explore how monomer selection and polymer architecture (for example, linear, branched, or crosslinked) influence molecular structure and enable the tailoring of mechanical, physical, and chemical properties. Core aspects of polymer physics are also addressed, such as chain dimensions, thermodynamics, and solution behaviour, together with the influence of bulk morphology and multicomponent systems on functional performance. The course further integrates polymer synthesis with key manufacturing methods for producing commodity and specialty plastics, and examines issues of recyclability, degradation, and environmental impact.

The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, laboratory activities and tests. 

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs.  It also provides foundational, polymer-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design.  

Previous knowledge of organic chemistry, thermodynamics and chemical reaction kinetics is required.
MATS3004.title: Polymer Science and Engineering 1

MATS3005.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the transformations that occur in metals, ceramics, and polymers, emphasising how these transformations can be exploited to control microstructure, thereby enhancing processability, properties, and overall performance.

The course begins by addressing the limitations of phase equilibria and introducing key concepts of time, driving force, and interfaces to explain transformation mechanisms and kinetics. It builds on fundamental principles of thermodynamics, diffusion, and kinetics to describe phase nucleation and growth, overall transformation kinetics, microstructural development, non-equilibrium phase formation, and the origin of isothermal and continuous cooling transformation diagrams. The course then covers liquid-to-solid transformations, examining solidification mechanisms, cast structure development, microsegregation (and homogenisation), interface stability, single crystal growth, glass formation and devitrification. It then extends to diffusional and non-diffusional solid-state transformation mechanisms, with applications to the formation of precipitates, pearlite, bainite, martensite and recrystallized microstructures.  Students will learn, through case studies, how transformations underpin modern materials manufacturing, from static and continuous casting of metals to polymer processing, glass manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, materials joining, additive manufacturing, and thermal or mechanical processing, and how these processes influence the resulting material structures and properties.  The case studies also demonstrate the ethical and sustainable approaches used in these industries.

The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, assignments, and tests. 

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program.  The foundational principles in the course underpin many of the key concepts covered in the accompanying Level 3 material-specific courses. 

Previous knowledge of crystallography, thermodynamics, phase equilibria, and transport phenomena is required.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2006 and MATS2008
MATS3005.title: Phase Transformations

MATS3006.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to essential computational tools for design and modelling in technological and professional materials engineering applications, emphasising the responsible and ethical use of data and simulations.  Selected computer simulation packages will be used to explore complex, real-world materials engineering phenomena.

Starting with an overview of computational materials modelling across length scales from the atomic to the macroscopic, this course will cover several important modelling techniques. Computer-aided design (CAD) will be introduced for precise geometry creation and virtual prototyping of material structures. Finite element analysis (FEA) will be applied to study temperature distributions, stress-strain behaviour, and mechanical integrity in materials with complex geometries, with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) used to analyse fluid flow and heat transfer in materials processing and performance applications. Finally, machine learning (ML) techniques, leveraging big data, will be introduced as a powerful technique for materials selection and discovery, property prediction, and the optimisation of processing conditions and performance characteristics. Together, these approaches form a foundational toolkit for more advanced studies in computational materials science and engineering.

The course includes lectures, high-level hands-on lab practices and an exam.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program.

Previous knowledge of computing and mathematics is required.
MATS3006.title: Design and Application of Materials in Science and Engineering 3

MATS3007.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with an integrated overview of key management concepts relevant to the materials engineering profession, including project management, risk management, marketing, and career development. Professional ethics is embedded throughout, with an emphasis on workplace expectations and ethical conduct.

The course begins with project management, where students learn about the project lifecycle, including planning, scheduling, reporting, stakeholder engagement and team dynamics. Students also develop a project plan relevant to the materials industry to demonstrate their ability to build a sound business case while meeting ethical and professional responsibilities in execution. This is followed by the principles of risk management, where students develop a risk management plan to accompany their project management plan.  Marketing is also addressed, including market analysis and product development, ensuring truthful representation and promoting sustainable business practices. Career development is an important part of a professional engineer’s journey, so the final part of the course focuses on job application strategies and résumé writing, all within the framework of ethical workplace behaviour.

The course includes lectures, including those delivered by academic guests, professionals and industry representatives, and tutorial sessions covering the key concepts of course components and related assessments.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program. It is also available as an Employability Experiences elective in the BSc program.
MATS3007.title: Materials Industry Management

MATS3008.description:
This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering builds on students’ prior knowledge of metals, ceramics, and polymers to demonstrate how composites and coatings with varying compositions and characteristics can be created from these individual constituents. The course emphasises the relationship between structure (microstructure & nanostructure) and processing for generating novel, advantageous properties in these materials for advanced structural and functional applications.

The course begins with an introduction to the types of composites (polymer-, ceramic-, and metal-matrix, nanocomposite, hybrid) and coatings (metal, ceramic, polymer, composite), as well as the different possible forms of the individual components in these composites (fibres, whiskers, and particulates). The course then covers the mechanical and physical properties of composites and coatings, the methods for testing these properties, and how they relate to the individual component materials and their forms, demonstrating how unique properties can emerge when individual materials are combined. The final part of the course covers fabrication routes for different types of composites and coatings, the impact of processing conditions on structure and properties, and strategies for recycling these materials for value-added applications.  Case studies are integrated throughout the course to illustrate the design of optimal composites and coatings for advanced structural and functional applications, while balancing performance with environmental responsibility and ethical industry practices.

The course will be delivered through lectures, assignments, laboratory activities, and tests.

This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program.  It also provides essential knowledge across the material classes for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design.

Previous knowledge of the structure-processing-property relationships for metals, ceramics, and polymers is required.
MATS3008.title: Design and Engineering of Composites and Coatings

MATS3199.description:
This course enables science students studying majors in the School of Materials Science and Engineering to apply their disciplinary knowledge and transferable skills in a professional context, through a work placement experience at an organisation external to UNSW. Students will have the opportunity to develop key professional skills that align with their career goals and contextualise their field of study in a professional workplace setting.

The main component of the course is a minimum 105-hour work placement related to the students field of study. The placement can be paid or unpaid. This supervised workplace experience is supported by professional development and discipline-specific modules that students can select from, in line with their individual career goals.

MATS3199 will count as a science or free elective and is graded on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.

Work placements are not guaranteed. Students are required to either apply for a faculty-advertised placement or submit an application for a self-sourced placement to be undertaken as part of the course, subject to approval. Further details on how to find and secure a work placement, the application and approval process, course content and assessments, can be found at: https://unsw.sharepoint.com/sites/Science-Student-Opportunities.

The course is available to domestic and international students.

Eligibility and Enrolment
Enrolment is subject to approval and completion of required pre-requisites. Permission to enrol will only be granted if the student:

  • is completing a Materials Science major in a Science program;
  • and has completed the required pre-requisites (48 units of credit, minimum 65 WAM, passed pre-requisite Preparation for WIL modules);
  • has secured a supervised work placement compatible to their major of study, which has been reviewed and approved by the School.

Please note:

  • The course is only available to students who are commencing a new work placement compatible to their major of study.
  • Students seeking to enrol with paid or unpaid work they are already undertaking outside their studies will not be considered.
  • Students are required to engage in recruitment activities and secure a relevant placement prior to seeking approval for enrolment.
  • It is the student’s responsibility to check if they have space in their program for this elective.
  • This course cannot be taken during an Honours year.
  • Overseas placements: In some cases, there may be overseas-based placements advertised by the Faculty. If a domestic or international student wishes to undertake a faculty-advertised overseas work placement, extra conditions will apply before the placement and enrolment into the course is approved. Self-sourced overseas placements are not permitted.

Prerequisite: enrolled in a Science program (single or dual) and majoring in Materials Science. Must pass Preparation for WIL modules prior to enrolment. Placement must be related to the student’s major, and approved by the School of Materials Science and Engineering prior to enrolment.
Pre-requisite: 48 units of credit and a minimum 65 WAM.
It is the student’s responsibility to check if they have space in their program for this elective. This course cannot be taken during an Honours year.
MATS3199.title: Materials Science Work Placement 1

This work placement course is for MATS students who wish to extend their work placement experience by completing a longer work placement (over two terms) or a more intensive placement (more hours in one term). Placements may be paid or unpaid. The three work placement options available to students are provided below -  the same eligibility and approval processes apply for all work placement options.   

  • Option A: 105-hour placement completed in 1 term; enrolment pattern = MATS3199; total of 6 UOC
  • Option B: 210-hour placement completed in 1 term; enrolment pattern = MATS3199 and MATS3299 in the same term; total of 12 UOC
  • Option C: 210-hour placement completed over 2 terms; enrolment pattern = MATS3199 in one term and MATS3299 in the following term; total of 12 UOC

In completing an extended or intensive option, students will have the opportunity to further develop professional workplace skills and engage in deeper self-reflection and analysis of the experience as a stepping stone into a graduate career.

MATS3299 will count as a science or free elective and is graded on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.

MATS4001.description:
This course will provide advanced knowledge in solidification, welding (emphasis on effect of welding on microstructure, HAZ etc.), fundamentals of metal working (including hot working, Zener-Hollomon parameter, dynamic recovery and recrystallization and cold working, formability, residual stresses, powder metallurgy and sintering, machining, recrystallisation phenomena. Emphasis on the effect of processing conditions on microstructure and hence properties. Common classes of magnesium alloys, copper alloys and cast irons to be taught illustrating some of the principles involved.

The course will be delivered through lectures and is for students in the final years of their materials science /and engineering degrees.
MATS4001.title: Secondary Processing of Metals

MATS4002.description:
This course is designed for 3rd, 4th or final year students undertaking studies in the discipline of materials science to enhance knowledge and understanding of advanced ceramics (oxides and non-oxides) for structural, thermal, electrical, piezoelectric, magnetic, optoelectronic, chemical, nuclear, biological, and wear applications. The contents will focus on fabrication of advanced materials in bulk and thin film format for use in these applications.   

The design of these materials will be focused in terms of the fundamental structure-microstructure-property relationships and how these can be tailored through alteration of the processing conditions to fabricate optimal advanced ceramics while reducing chances of failure.  This will be achieved through use of case studies and examples related to the design of these advanced ceramics for superior mechanical properties (strength, modulus, and toughness), electrical (dielectric, ferroelectric, piezoelectric), magnetic (ferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic), electromechanical, optoelectronic, tribological (wear resistance), thermal (expansion, conductivity, heat capacity), thermomechanical (thermal shock, refractoriness), chemical (corrosive), nuclear (radiation resistance), and biological (bioaffinity).
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS3002
MATS4002.title: Design and Advanced Ceramics

MATS4004.description:
This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering will further develop capabilities in fracture mechanics and fractography for students with a Materials or general Engineering background. 

Fracture is the most common form of engineering failure, costing the global economy enormous amounts of money as well as many lives.  Through a combination of lectures, tutorials, laboratories and project work, students will develop advanced knowledge fracture mechanics.  Understanding methods for calculating stress distributions in real-world components, risks for fracture initiation, fatigue and lifetime analysis, and materials degradation mechanisms provides engineers with the tools for the design of components that can operate safely for known time-periods.  By applying forensic fractographic analysis, students will learn how to identify the causes of fracture in real industrial-scale failures.

Previous knowledge of mechanical properties of materials is required.
MATS4004.title: Fracture Mechanics and Failure Analysis

MATS4005.description:
This course is designed for 3rd, 4th or final year students undertaking studies in the materials science discipline or combined degrees with materials science.

The course aims to enhance knowledge and understanding of two important categories of advanced materials, namely functional materials and composite materials. The classes will comprise of lectures focusing on key topics in these fields, relevant laboratory activities, and design problems related to materials design in these fields.

The functional materials part will focus on fabrication of functional materials in different nanostructural forms (0D, 1D, 2D, MOFs, and composite bulk forms) and design of these materials in advanced devices and applications such as catalysts, batteries, fuel cells, supercapacitors, pseudocapacitors, superconductors, semiconducting devices, photovoltaics, and biosensors)

The composite materials part will focus on different types of composites (polymer, metal, and ceramic matrix composites), their fabrication routes, importance of their properties (strength, modulus, fracture etc.), failure mechanisms in the bulk and individual components, recycling methods, and designing composite materials for different applications (structural and non-structural).
MATS4005.title: Composites and Functional Materials

MATS4006.description: The course focuses on advanced polymers, including but not limited to polymers in dielectrics, optoelectronics, solar technology, and medicine. It expands on concepts taught in MATS3004 Polymer Science and Engineering I. Students will learn about polymerization techniques used to produce polymers and copolymers with enhanced functionalities, the rubber elasticity theory that governs the behavior of elastomeric materials and networks, and the rheological property of polymer melts critical for their industrial processing. The course also covers failure mode of polymeric products while in usage. The course includes lab activities intended as a practical companion to the concepts taught in the lectures, thereby, enabling the student with a technology-enhanced learning experience.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS3004
MATS4006.title: Polymer Science and Engineering 2

MATS4007.description:
Degradation of engineering materials occurs most commonly through corrosion and wear. This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering teaches students how to minimise and control the rate at which these occur to extend the lifespan of engineering components. The course is taught through lectures and laboratories and covers three main areas:

Corrosion and Control Strategies: Corrosion occurs in several ways. Students will learn the causes of each type of corrosion, and how to prevent corrosion, or reduce the rate at which corrosion occurs in established systems.

Wear: Wear occurs in many engineering applications. Students will learn about the primary mechanisms by which wear occurs, and how simple models of these wear mechanisms allow the main parameters and materials properties affecting wear rates to be identified.

Surface Engineering: Students will learn about the purpose of engineered surfaces to increase the lifespan of materials by increasing resistance to both corrosion and wear, with a focus on the hardening of steel and the common coating methods used in industry to protect different materials.

Previous knowledge of thermodynamics, kinetics, and mechanical properties is required.
MATS4007.title: Engineered Surfaces to Resist Corrosion and Wear

MATS4100.description:
This course is only available to students enrolled in the School of Materials Science and Engineering BE Honours Program and must be taken in each term of Honours. The School’s Honours Coordinator must approve enrolment.

A self-directed experimental research or design-based project to apply, contextualise, and integrate fundamental scientific/engineering concepts learnt throughout the Materials Science and Engineering undergraduate program. Students will develop advanced disciplinary knowledge and will apply this to problem solving in the chosen topic area. Students will develop and practice high-level skills in critical thinking, project management, safety consideration and risk management, data collection and analysis, problem solving, and technical communication.
Note: this course is 18 UOC in total: 6 UOC per term over three terms.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: MATS3001 and MATS3002 and MATS3004
MATS4100.title: Materials Engineering Project

MATS4503.description: This course provides students with formal training in professional communication, writing skills, project planning, data analysis, intellectual property, risk management, and workplace health and safety.  These skills directly underpin the Materials Science Honours Project (MATS4505) and are essential for any science graduate.  The course is only available to students enrolled in the School of Materials Science and Engineering Honours Program, and must be taken in a student’s first term of Honours in conjunction with a Science Honours research project in the School of Materials Science and Engineering. The School’s Honours Coordinator must approve enrolment.  The course is completed as weekly lectures, self-learning activities, and seminar presentations.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolled in Materials Science Honours Plan
MATS4503.title: Professional Skills

MATS4504.description:
This course is only available to students enrolled in the School of Materials Science and Engineering Honours Program and must be taken in a student’s first Term of Honours in conjunction with the Materials Science Honours Project course (MATS4505). The School’s Honours Coordinator must approve enrolment.

This course and MATS4503 Professional Skills provide essential introduction to Honours for Science students undertaking a full-time Science Honours program in the School of Materials Science and Engineering. MATS4503 consists of 30 hours of class contact hours and students are expected to take an additional 120 hours of non-class hours spread over the term to complete study and readings, undertake critical review of literature and develop a project proposal, and preparation for seminar. The course results in a written research proposal providing an account of relevant scientific literature and a description of the research work expected to be undertaken during the Honours program, and a short seminar presentation to present these to a scientific audience. The focus of the research proposal is decided in consultation with the student’s Honours Supervisor and is related to the topic area of the research project. Students will also present a short seminar based on their proposal
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolled in Materials Science Honours Plan
MATS4504.title: Research Training

MATS4505.description:
In this course, students will complete a self-directed experimental research project to apply, contextualise, and integrate fundamental scientific concepts learnt throughout the Materials Science undergraduate program. Students will develop advanced disciplinary knowledge and will apply this to research and problem solving in the chosen topic area. Students will develop and practice high-level skills in information searching and retrieval, planning and execution of scientific work, safety and risk management, critical thinking, data collection and analysis, problem solving, and written and oral scientific communication.
Note: This course is available only to students enrolled in a full-time Honours year in the Materials Science specialisation in Programs 4500 BSci(Hons) and 3962 BAdvSci(Hons) and is run over three terms (3 x 12 UoC for a total of 36 UoC). The course is taken with MATS4503 Professional Skills (6 UoC) and MATS4504 Research Training (6 UoC) to comprise the 48 UoC Honours year.
enrolment_rules_raw: Prerequisite: Enrolled in MATSCH Materials Science Honours specialisation in the Science (Honours) or Advanced Science (Honours) program including double-degrees
MATS4505.title: Materials Science Honours Project

MATS6007.description: This postgraduate course will give an overview of the materials footprint on environment during their life cycle, from extraction to disposal. Through a series of lectures, students will learn a range of different approaches towards creating a sustainable system and explore how these approaches can improve sustainability and minimise environmental impact of diverse types of materials (metals, ceramics, polymers and composites) in different sectors (i.e., transportation, infrastructure, and energy generation/storage).
MATS6007.title: Sustainable Materials Engineering

MDCN8000.description:
Note: MDCN8000 (6 UOC) is a multi-term course run over 3-terms for a total UOC of 18. MDCN8000 is only available to students undertaking our Course Work intensive Honours program (18 UOC from research and 30 UOC from Coursework). 

The learning and teaching philosophy underpinning this course is centred on BSc (Med) Hons students taking on the role of researcher. In doing so, they develop advanced disciplinary knowledge, the use of specialised techniques/methodology relevant to their chosen research area, critical thinking, evaluation and synthesis of information, in addition to scientific research communication in the oral and written forms.

The principal form of teaching is based on research supervision and direction by specialist researchers within UNSW Medicine. Complementary to this, online Research Skills modules will be delivered and have been designed to provide training to BSc (Med) Hons students in diverse areas that constitute research practice. Learning outcomes from this course will form the basis for future pursuits in medical research and transferrable skills.

The information for this course is in the form of experimental techniques, protocols, technical tips and materials, which are usually provided by each research environment and supervisor. In addition, self-directed use of other resources such as web-based sources are expected. You will need to maintain consistent communication with your supervisor and actively seek assistance from your supervisor or co-supervisor to clarify your understanding, as required.
